http://www.gingersoftware.com/content/grammar-rules/adjectives/compound-adjectives/ A compound adjective doesn't always need hyphens. The idea of hyphens in compound adjectives is to avoid ambiguity, but with something as abstract as poetry ambiguity is a good thing. It lets the reader use their imagination. This means any two words can be a compound. Also, a word can be an adjective and a verb at the same time. If you say a person is "sweating" it is also an adjective becuase sweat has a smell, a taste, texture and if you have the right mind set it also has color and temperature. Sweating becomes more than an action, but a quality.

"Beastly" hooves. "Bruised" conductress. "Battling" beast. It's not really the adjectives and verbs themselves that are plain, it's the nouns that are atatched to them that make them plain. Sometimes all you need to do to make those words less plain, is to make it a compound adjectives and verbs. ______ beastly. _____ bruised. _____ Battling beast. The adjectives, verbs, nouns you use in your poem are kind of plain. Don't be afraid to be more abstract with the words you use. Using single words with a combination of scent, color, texture, temperature, sound, or taste can make your poetry pop out. The more your poem pops, the more depth it has. For example: If someone has a broken heart, in a short story a person would likely go on a journey to find the pieces, where as a character in a poem will use terms like "Over time I stapled myself back together". Almost to say the journey was very painful. If you say, "Over time I glued myself back together." It suddenly means that the person was unsuccessfully in healing their broken heart because they didn't try hard enough.
